hints: Look carefully at the two curves. Which one should you use for the lungs where carbon dioxide is low, and which one for active tissue where carbon dioxide is high?

Remember the Bohr shift. High carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin affinity for oxygen, so the curve shifts to the right. Now read saturation at $100 \text{ mmHg}$ on the left curve and at $35 \text{ mmHg}$ on the right curve.
walkthrough:
**Decide which curve is which**

Think like haemoglobin. In the lungs, $CO_2$ is low, so affinity for oxygen is high and loading is easy. In active tissue, $CO_2$ is high, so affinity is lower and unloading is easy.

Rule to remember: high $CO_2$ shifts the curve to the right (Bohr effect). So the upper left curve is lungs, the lower right curve is active tissue.

**Read the lungs value at 100 mmHg**

Go to $100 \text{ mmHg}$ on the x-axis and go straight up to the upper (lungs) curve. Then go across to the y-axis.

Reading:
$$\text{saturation at lungs} \approx 94\%$$

**Read the active tissue value at 35 mmHg**

Now go to $35 \text{ mmHg}$ on the x-axis, but this time go up to the lower (active tissue) curve because $CO_2$ is high there. Then go across to the y-axis.

Reading:
$$\text{saturation at tissue} \approx 40\%$$
That large drop from 94% to 40% shows lots of oxygen has been released where it is needed.

options.A: Tissue value of 40 is correct, but 92 is too low for the lungs. At 100 mmHg the upper curve reads about 94, not 92.
options.B: Both readings use the wrong curve. 92 is low for lungs and 66 is the resting tissue value from the upper curve, not the right-shifted active tissue curve.
options.C: Correct. Lungs on the upper curve at 100 mmHg gives about 94%, and active tissue on the lower right-shifted curve at 35 mmHg gives about 40%.
options.D: Lungs value of 94 is correct, but 66 is read from the upper lungs curve at 35 mmHg. Active tissue must be read from the lower Bohr-shifted curve, giving about 40.
